text.p: South Australian Premier John Olsen's pressing target to revive business investment in his state received a boost last week with an A$300 million city centre development proposal led by David Jones Ltd.

It would, he said, put the state back on the investment map, but it will come at the cost of one of SA's oldest department stores, John Martin's, and up to 300 jobs before construction is due to start and benefits to flow in.

In the meantime, Olsen -- in the state's top job for just three months -- faces two critical campaigns: an election and a drive to convince his federal colleagues to go easy on the automotive industry, which underpins the SA economy.
"I would concede this economy has a long way to go," he told Reuters in a recent interview.
"My concern is the debate about (automotive) tariffs is now putting an element of uncertainty about investment and I think South Australia can ill afford to have that kind of uncertainty," he said.

Olsen said that while private capital investment in SA rose 27.3 percent in the two years to March 1996, beating government targets, its growth had slowed to 2.2 percent in the 12 months to September 1996, compared to the national rate of 14.2 percent.

Olsen achieved his long-held ambition to be premier last November when Dean Brown, who led the Liberal Party to power in 1993, was ousted in an eruption of long-term internal rivalries and backbench concern about poor opinion polls and the economy.

His short period in office has been marked by the leaking -- reportedly from a senior Liberal source -- of 800 pages of sensitive documents and the resignation of his finance and mines minister Dale Baker, pending a conflict of interest inquiry by police.
With the budget to be handed down on May 29, Olsen said the government's targets -- an A$60 million underlying deficit in 1996/97 and an A$10 million surplus in 1997/98 -- remain intact.
Other targets are to revive investment, further boost exports, and bring SA's unemployment, which has hovered around 9.5 percent, closer to the national average of 8.5 percent.

Olsen says there are some encouraging signs in the economy: a second consecutive good harvest, WMC Ltd's decision to expand copper and uranium production at Olympic Dam, a A$200 million oil and gas exploration program by Santos Ltd and a boom in exploration in the mining hotspot, the Gawler Craton.

Meanwhile he says the housing industry reported a rise in building approvals in January, motor vehicle sales were also up in January, and the retail industry had seen "some degree of tentative consumer confidence returning."
"There is some sign of movement (in the economy, but) there is a long way to go," Olsen said.
"We need to ensure there is economic rejuvenation this year: that is being impeded by a broad lack of community confidence."

Confidence, it appears, is the key word, and is offered also by many local business leaders as a critical failure here, much still in the wake of the disastrous A$3 billion collapse of the State Bank under the former Labor administration in 1992.
The government has raised A$1.8 billion in asset sales over three years and reduced public sector net debt to 22 percent of gross state product in 1996 from 28.1 percent in 1992.

But while Olsen initiated the A$1.5 billion outsourcing of the State's water supply, he remains, publicly at least, unattracted to privatising options for SA's last big-ticket item, the Electricity Trust (ETSA).
"Cabinet has given no consideration to, we have embraced no policy that incorporates (privatisation, partial sale or outsourcing of ETSA operations)," he said.
He rejects any fear of political backlash for the stand, saying ETSA has shown itself, unlike SAWater, to be a performer.
In another corporate matter, Olsen said any plan to lift the 15 percent single shareholder ceiling in Santos Ltd, designed as a takeover defence, was "not under consideration".
While local media still speculate a State poll could be held in April or May, Olsen suggested it is unlikely to be held before December, the Liberals' fourth anniversary in office.

Nonetheless next month will see him in campaign mode, in support of the car industry as the Productivity Commission holds public hearings on responses to its proposal to cut tariffs to five percent by 2004 from the current 25 percent.

There is debate over whether tariff cuts would really put at risk automotive investment in Australia, as the industry has claimed, but with SA home to two big employing manufacturers -- Holden Automotive and Mitsubishi -- Olsen's options are limited.
As one local economist put it: "I don't think John Olsen can afford to not believe the car industry."
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373 1800
